1. Tally plus spreadsheets plus WhatsApp

What most Indian businesses of this size run today, and it is not stupid. Tally is good at what it does, your CA already works in it, and the auditor asks for it by name. What it costs is not the licence — it is that sales lives in WhatsApp, stock lives in a sheet, invoices live in Tally, and every month somebody decides which of the three was right.

It breaks on volume and geography. Two locations means two counts and no single available figure. Thirty-odd orders a month means the sheet is right on Monday and roughly right by Wednesday. And nothing in that stack will tell you the input tax credit you are about to claim is not in GSTR-2B.

  • Choose this instead of us if you are under ten people, on one site, under about thirty orders a month, and nobody spends more than half a day a month reconciling. You do not have a systems problem yet.
  • We do not ask you to leave Tally either way. Ordence exports vouchers into it with deterministic remote IDs, so a re-export updates rather than duplicates. Most customers keep the statutory books there on purpose.

2. Zoho One or a similar mid-market suite

The closest thing to a real competitor here. Forty-plus apps, published SOC 2 and ISO certifications, and a per-user price that looks very reasonable. What surprises people is that a suite is a box of parts: somebody has to decide how CRM talks to Books talks to Inventory, build the flows, and keep them working. That person is a partner you pay by the hour, or an employee who quietly becomes the Zoho administrator.

It breaks for us on Indian statutory depth. Section 17(5) blocked credit shown beside claimable credit before you file. Section 43B(h) turning a 45-day MSME payment into a disallowed expense. Section 206AB doubling a TDS rate. Those cost real money, and a general suite treats them as a field.

  • Choose Zoho instead of us if you need breadth we do not have: helpdesk, marketing automation, HR, expenses, all under one login.
  • Choose Zoho if procurement requires SOC 2 or ISO 27001. They have it, we do not, and we will not imply otherwise with a badge.
  • Choose Zoho if you operate in more than one country, or if you have someone in-house who enjoys configuring software. Without that person a suite becomes forty apps with three in use.

3. Building it with a freelancer or an in-house developer

Looks cheapest and most often is not. The first version lands roughly on time and does exactly what you asked. Then the requirements you did not think of arrive, and each one is a change request against code one person understands.

What you do not get: tenant isolation you can prove, an audit trail, backups anyone has restored under pressure. We enforce isolation in the database with row-level security rather than in application code, and run a double-entry ledger a trigger refuses to let go out of balance. That is not what gets built in a three-month engagement. And the real cost is the bus factor — we have inherited that project several times.

  • Choose a build instead of us if the requirement is one narrow workflow nobody sells: a specific configurator, a specific pricing engine, something genuinely peculiar to how you make money.
  • Choose a build if you already employ two or more developers and intend to keep doing so. Then it is a team, not a bus factor, and you should own your core system.

4. SAP Business One or Odoo with an implementation partner

Real ERPs run by real partners, and for a business at the top of our range and growing hard they may be the right call. Multi-level material planning, shop-floor scheduling, consolidation across entities and currencies. We do none of that.

It does not break — that is the honest thing to say. What happens instead is a 30-person trading business ends up with a system built for a 300-person manufacturer, and the gap is filled with consultant days for as long as they own it.

  • Choose a tier-one ERP if you consolidate multiple legal entities, or operate across countries and currencies.
  • Choose it if you genuinely manufacture. Ordence handles a simple bill of materials and simple work orders; beyond that we would be selling you a disappointment.
  • Choose it if a lender or a parent company has mandated a named system, or if you need a bench of forty consultants and a follow-the-sun desk.

Where Ordence loses, before you find out yourself

This list costs us deals. Finding it in month two of an implementation is worse than reading it now.

  • No SOC 2 and no ISO 27001. If procurement requires a certificate we fail today.
  • No single sign-on, no self-serve signup, no free trial.
  • No public API and no developer portal. Automations can call out under a strict policy; nothing calls in.
  • No offline mobile app. It works properly on a phone in a browser, which is a different thing.
  • We are small. We would rather tell you we have no capacity until March than take your money and be late.

Questions people actually ask

You have listed four competitors fairly. What is the catch?

An incentive, not a catch. A customer who signs after reading this page has expectations that match what we built, and those are the only implementations that go well.

We are already on Zoho or Odoo. Is moving worth it?

Often not, and we will say so. If the system works and your team is in it daily, the cost of moving is real and the benefit marginal. The migrations worth doing are the ones where people have quietly gone back to spreadsheets.

What if we compare properly and pick someone else?

Then you made a good decision with better information. Tell us who and why if you are willing — it is the most useful thing anyone sends us.

Bring us the comparison you have already started.

The spreadsheet with three vendors and a column of question marks. We will fill in our column honestly, including the rows where the answer is no.
